headline: 3D-printed F-14 Tomcat uses FPGA recreation of the ‘world’s first microprocessor, the MP944
summary: An FPGA recreation of the F-14's Central Air Data Computer (CADC) now controls the swing-wing system of a 3D-printed model. This CADC was powered by the MP944, a chip some argue predates Intel's 4004.
details: FPGA and embedded systems expert Alan Taylor has successfully recreated the U.S. Navy’s F-14 Tomcat’s Central Air Data Computer (CADC) in an FPGA. This system was tested by controlling the articulated sweep-wing system of a 3D-printed scale model of the F-14 Tomcat.

The CADC is renowned for being the core intelligence behind the F-14's advanced fighter capabilities. Its brain was the MP944 microprocessor, which some historians contend was the world's first, beginning service in June 1970, over a year before Intel's 4004.

Despite its early deployment, the MP944 remained an official secret until 1998, allowing the Intel 4004 to gain widespread recognition as the first microprocessor. The MP944 was a 20-bit, pipelined, parallel multi-microprocessor, running at 375 kHz and executing 9,375 instructions per second.

Designed by Steve Geller, Ray Holt, and a 25-strong team, the chip passed stringent ruggedness tests, capable of operating in temperatures from -55 to +125 degrees Celsius. It functioned as part of a six-chip system within the CADC, calculating real-time flight parameters like altitude and airspeed.

This innovation was crucial for enabling the Tomcat’s articulated sweep-wing system. Chip architecture enthusiasts assert the MP944 was significantly faster than the Intel 4004, which was originally designed for a desktop calculator.

Alan Taylor's project provides a full open-source set of VHDL source code, documentation, and testbenches for an FPGA recreation of the F-14’s CADC. The GitHub repository includes complete synthesizable VHDL implementations for all six original CADC chips, utilizing a Spartan-7 based SoM.

headline_marked: [[Hugging Face highlights top AI papers]]: self-improving agents, Ascend LLM training, and K-12 education
headline: Hugging Face highlights top AI papers: self-improving agents, Ascend LLM training, and K-12 education
summary: This month's selection features breakthroughs in recursively self-improving AI agents, large language model post-training on Ascend SuperPODs, and curriculum-aligned LLMs for K-12 education.
details: Hugging Face's latest top AI papers span diverse fields, from recursively self-improving agents to large language model training on non-NVIDIA hardware and curriculum-aligned LLMs for education.

One notable paper, AREX, introduces a recursively self-improving agent. Instead of just answering queries, it can detect its own weaknesses and refine its reasoning and information gathering processes over time.

Another key paper, SLAI T-Rex, addresses the NVIDIA CUDA dependency by demonstrating full-parameter post-training for DeepSeek-V4 models on Ascend SuperPOD infrastructure. This proves the feasibility of large-scale fine-tuning outside the prevalent NVIDIA ecosystem.

A third paper focuses on improving LLMs for K-12 education, tackling the issue of models providing seemingly correct but curriculum-misaligned answers. It proposes building a knowledge graph aligned with the K-12 curriculum.
